To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the structural equation theories of causation are not consistent with the folk attributions of causation.

(i) theories of actual causality that use structural equations and directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to model causal relationships are meant to satisfy a widely-endors-ed folk attribution desiderata (FAD) and (ii) these theories fail to do so in several cases.

(i) theories that supplement the graphical machinery with considerations of typicality and normality fail to agree with the reports of untored individuals about specific cases; (ii) theories that supplement this machinery with considerations of defaults and normality do not agree with the reports from untutored individuals for the cases we consider, but (iii) they do so if we replace the consideration of typicality with the consideration of norms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
two issues: (1) the extent to which folk attributions of causal responsibility can be used to evaluate theories of actual causality; and (2) the nature of these folk attributions themselves.
how to make the best use of the folk attribution desiderata in developing theories of actual causality.
the relationship between folk intuitions about causation and the formal models that have been proposed to capture those intuitions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the FAD is satisfied by the structural equations approach to causation, but not by its typicality or normality-based supplements.
the FAD is a good thing, and that the structural equation approach to causation can be made to satisfy the Fad, but only if we give up on typicality and focus instead on injunctive norms.

we have shown that the FAD cannot be satisfied in the way that many theorists would like, and that the only way to satisfy it is to give up the typicality and normality considerations that are so central to the theories of Pearl and Hitchcock.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the FAD should be abandoned in favor of a responsibility-based desideratum.

, in order for theories of actual causality to be in line with the way folk attributions work, the theories should take into account the injunctive norms that people use to evaluate the actions and outcomes of others.

the FAD is a useful constraint on the acceptibility of a theory of causation only if the theory can account for the relevant folk attributions in a way that does not rely on the typicality of the cause or effect.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order for a theory to satisfy the FAd, it must be sensitive to both descriptive and prescriptive norms.
, if one is interested in the FAD, one should not assume that the folk have a theory of causation in the first place.
, in addition to the FAD, a good theory of causation should be able to accommodate the folk’s tendency to make causal attributions that reflect the norms and standards of the relevant social group.
